The integration of edge computing with artificial intelligence has emerged as a transformative paradigm in precision agriculture. This convergence addresses a critical limitation in conventional IoT-based farming systems: the reliance on cloud connectivity for data processing and decision-making. In many agricultural regions, particularly in developing economies, intermittent network connectivity and high latency render cloud-dependent architectures impractical for time-sensitive operations such as irrigation scheduling and plant health monitoring.

Moreover, the proposed system architecture leverages the computational capabilities of the Raspberry Pi 4, which serves as the primary edge computing node. An Arduino Uno microcontroller is employed for analog sensor data acquisition, and environmental parameters including soil moisture content, ambient temperature, relative humidity, and atmospheric pressure are monitored using calibrated sensors at ten-minute intervals. A Raspberry Pi Camera Module V2 captures visual data for plant health assessment using a convolutional neural network.

The experimental design follows a three-zone configuration to evaluate system performance. The control zone operates under conventional timer-based irrigation. The stress zone receives reduced irrigation at seventy percent of the control volume. The AI-managed zone uses predictive irrigation scheduling driven by a Random Forest model. Roma VF tomato plants serve as the test crop across all three zones.

In addition, the system utilizes a Random Forest machine learning algorithm for predictive irrigation scheduling. This algorithm analyzes historical sensor data and weather patterns to optimize water usage. A Convolutional Neural Network is deployed for plant health assessment. The experimental methodology employed a randomized controlled trial design to ensure statistical validity.

Preliminary results indicate that the AI-managed zone achieved a twenty-three percent reduction in water consumption compared to the timer-based control, while maintaining statistically equivalent plant health metrics. Soil moisture variance in the AI-managed zone remained within optimal ranges for ninety-four percent of the trial duration. It is worth noting that the system's performance was validated through comprehensive testing in controlled environmental conditions.

Several limitations warrant acknowledgment. The six-week trial period does not capture seasonal variations in weather patterns or crop growth stages. Sensor drift over extended deployment periods was not fully characterised. Additionally, the CNN-based plant health assessment model was trained on a limited dataset of two thousand images captured under controlled lighting conditions. Future work should focus on validating the system in diverse agricultural environments.
